opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a direction I find really exciting, and honestly a bit underexplored relative to how intuitive it is. The core idea is simple: not every token deserves the same amount of compute. If you're predicting "the" after "on top of," you don't need to run through eighty layers with the full width of the model. But if you're in the middle of a tricky reasoning step or a math derivation, you probably want more. Today's dense transformers spend exactly the same FLOPs on both, which feels wasteful.

There's been a lot of interesting work here. Early exit approaches, where you attach classifiers at intermediate layers and stop when you're confident. Mixture-of-Depths, where tokens can route around blocks. And in a sense Mixture-of-Experts is a cousin of this idea, though it's really about conditional parameters rather than conditional compute per token; each token still uses roughly the same FLOPs. Then there are the recurrent-depth or looped transformer ideas, where you can iterate a block more times for harder inputs.

My honest assessment is that it's promising, but it hasn't yet clearly won at scale. A few reasons. One is hardware: GPUs love regular, batched, dense computation. Once tokens take different paths, you get load-balancing problems and irregular memory access, and the theoretical FLOP savings often don't turn into wall-clock savings. Another is training stability, since the routing decisions are discrete and harder to learn well. And the bar keeps moving: every time someone shows a gain, the dense baseline gets better recipes and more data, and the gap shrinks.

The other thing I'd point out is that we've found a different way to get adaptive compute that works really well in practice: reasoning in token space. When a model thinks longer with chain of thought, it's spending more compute on harder problems. That's adaptive computation, just at the sequence level rather than inside the architecture. It's crude in a way, since you're forcing everything through discrete tokens, but it's extremely effective and it's compatible with existing infrastructure.

So I think the interesting open question is whether we can combine the two: models that reason in a latent space, adapt their depth internally, and only surface tokens when they need to. I'd expect that to come back in a big way once someone makes it efficient on real hardware. But right now, if you asked me where to bet for the next model, I'd still bet on dense or MoE plus test-time reasoning, with architectural adaptivity as the research bet that could pay off later.

r001.rationale: The response says adaptive computation has not clearly won at scale, but does not state that the speaker knows of no work that has successfully achieved it.

r002.rationale: It mentions recurrent-depth or looped transformers, but does not identify the Universal Transformer or describe it as choosing layer repetitions based on token complexity.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, adaptive computation is one of those ideas that everyone agrees is obviously right in principle, and yet it keeps failing to become the default. The intuition is simple: not every token deserves the same amount of compute. Predicting "the" after "of" is trivial, while predicting the next step of a proof or the right function call is not. A fixed-depth transformer spends exactly the same FLOPs on both, which is wasteful.

The research history goes back a long way. Adaptive Computation Time from Alex Graves, Universal Transformers, PonderNet, early-exit methods, and more recently mixture-of-depths, where you route only a subset of tokens through each block. All of these show something, usually a nice efficiency curve on a benchmark. And then they mostly don't survive contact with production.

I think there are three reasons. First, hardware. GPUs love uniform, dense, predictable work. The moment tokens take different paths, you get load imbalance, ragged batches, and all your theoretical FLOP savings get eaten by the systems overhead. Mixture-of-experts only succeeded because people did the painful engineering to make routing efficient at scale, and it took years.

Second, training dynamics. The routing decision is discrete, so you need tricks to make it learnable, and those tricks tend to be unstable or introduce a gap between training and inference. It's hard to get a clean signal for "this token needed more thought."

Third, and this is the one I find most interesting: the field found a different answer to the same question. Chain of thought and test-time compute with reasoning models are adaptive computation, just at the sequence level instead of inside the architecture. The model decides to think longer by emitting more tokens. It's a crude mechanism, but it works with existing hardware, it works with existing training stacks, and you can reinforce it with RL. So the pressure to solve adaptivity inside the layers dropped, because we got most of the benefit through a mechanism that was much easier to deploy.

Where I'd place the state of research today: it's a healthy, somewhat underrated direction that I expect to come back, because reasoning traces are very expensive at inference time. You end up spending thousands of tokens of full-depth compute where a smarter architecture could make the easy steps cheap. The sweet spot is probably a hybrid, where the model allocates depth per token and also decides how much to externalize into text. But to be honest, nobody has yet shown a convincing result at frontier scale where the architectural version clearly beats just scaling a dense model and training it to reason. Until that result exists, it stays a research topic rather than a recipe.

r001.rationale: The response says prior approaches show benchmark efficiency gains but usually do not reach production, and that no architectural method has convincingly beaten dense reasoning at frontier scale. It does not state that the speaker knows of no work that has successfully achieved token-complexity-adaptive computation.

r002.rationale: The response names Universal Transformers but does not explain that they choose how many times to apply a layer based on token complexity.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very interesting direction, because we currently spend roughly the same amount of computation on every token, and clearly not every token requires the same amount of reasoning. Sometimes you’re just completing an obvious phrase; sometimes the next token depends on solving a difficult problem.

But I would distinguish the intuition from whether we’ve found a practical architecture that delivers on it. You need a way to learn when to spend more compute, and you need that flexibility to translate into actual efficiency. If different tokens take different paths or different numbers of steps, that can make batching more complicated. Saving computation on paper doesn’t necessarily mean reducing latency.

So I’m optimistic about the direction, but I’d judge it by a fairly concrete question: at the same compute budget, does it produce better answers? And can you preserve that advantage when you scale it up and serve it? That’s where the architectural idea has to prove itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the challenge of making adaptive computation practical, but does not state that the speaker knows of no work that has achieved it.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention the Universal Transformer or an architecture choosing how many times to apply a layer based on token complexity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very promising direction. Today, we spend roughly the same amount of computation on every token, even though some tokens are very easy to predict and others require much more reasoning. That seems inefficient.

But there are different ways to make computation adaptive. You can change how much of the network is activated, how many layers a token goes through, or how much time the model spends generating and refining an answer. Those approaches don’t all solve the same problem.

The challenge is learning when extra computation is useful. You also have to translate theoretical savings into actual speed: if every token takes a different path, batching and hardware utilization become harder. So I’m optimistic, but I would judge progress by the quality you get for a given compute budget, including the practical cost of running the system.

r001.rationale: The speaker calls the direction promising and describes its challenges, but does not say they know of no work that has successfully adapted computation to token complexity.

r002.rationale: The response discusses varying network activation and layer count, but does not identify the Universal Transformer or explain its token-dependent layer application.
